A2.text:
Murad wanted to ask his girlfriend, Aysel, to marry him. He had a plan. On Saturday evening, they would walk on the Boulevard by the sea, and he would give her the ring there.

On Friday, Murad checked the forecast. “Sunny and warm, with a light breeze,” it said. Perfect!

But on Saturday, the sky was grey. First there was a little drizzle. Murad was very worried. He called his friend Tural.

“Calm down,” Tural said. “It is just a little rain. This is a storm in a teacup.”

In the evening, Murad met Aysel. He was pale and quiet.

“Are you okay?” Aysel asked. “You look a bit under the weather.”

“I'm fine,” Murad said, but his hands were shaking.

They walked by the sea. Suddenly, there was a heavy downpour. They ran to a bus stop. Their shoes were wet and the wind was freezing.

Murad thought, “It is now or never.” He took out the small box. But his hands were cold, and the ring fell into a big puddle!

Murad looked at the water in horror. Aysel started to laugh. She picked up the ring from the puddle and put it on her finger.

“Yes,” she said. “Come rain or shine, the answer is yes.”

Murad proposes in the rain, and Aysel says yes

B1.text:
Murad had planned everything. After a long, humid summer and a week-long heatwave in August, October in Baku was finally cool and calm. On Saturday evening he would walk with his girlfriend Aysel along the Boulevard, stop at their favourite bench by the sea and ask her to marry him.

On Friday night he checked the forecast three times. “Clear skies, light breeze.” He slept like a baby.

On Saturday morning, he woke to a grey sky and a fine drizzle against the window. By lunchtime he was walking around his flat in circles. He phoned his friend Tural.

“The whole plan is ruined,” he moaned.

“Murad, it's a bit of rain,” said Tural. “You're making a storm in a teacup. She's marrying you, not the weather.”

At seven, Murad met Aysel at the metro. He was so nervous that he couldn't finish a sentence.

“Are you all right?” she asked, touching his forehead. “You look a bit under the weather.”

“Just tired,” he lied.

They had only reached the Carpet Museum when the sky opened. It wasn't rain any more; it was a proper downpour. They ran, laughing and screaming, to a bus stop, where the wind off the sea was freezing.

Water was dripping from his hair, but Murad decided it was now or never. He went down on one knee, opened the little box — and his cold fingers dropped the ring straight into a puddle.

For a second, neither of them moved. Then Aysel bent down, fished the ring out of the dirty water and slipped it onto her finger.

“You know what?” she said, smiling. “I'll walk with you come rain or shine. Yes.”

An old man waiting for the bus started clapping. Behind the clouds, the sun was already coming back.

options: A proposal that goes wrong because of the weather, but still ends happily
A couple who hate the rain

questions.why: “It's a bit of rain... She's marrying you, not the weather.”

questions.why: He saw Aysel put on the ring and say yes.

B2.text:
Murad had rehearsed the proposal more thoroughly than his university finals. Baku had just come through a sticky, humid summer, capped by a heatwave that kept everyone indoors for most of August, and October had arrived like an apology: soft light, a gentle breeze off the Caspian, evenings made for walking. On Saturday, he would take Aysel along the Boulevard to the bench where they'd had their first proper conversation, and there — with the sea turning pink behind them — he would ask her to marry him.

The forecast on Friday night was flawless: clear skies, light winds. He checked it three times anyway and slept soundly for the first time in a week.

He woke to a sky the colour of wet cement and a persistent drizzle tapping at the window. By noon he had refreshed four weather apps and was pacing the flat. Eventually he rang his friend Tural.

“The whole thing's ruined,” he said.

“You're making a storm in a teacup,” Tural replied. “It's drizzle, Murad. She's agreeing to spend her life with you, not to go to the beach.”

When he met Aysel outside the metro at seven, he was so distracted that he greeted her twice. She studied him with narrowed eyes. “You look under the weather. Are you coming down with something?”

“Long week,” he said vaguely.

They had made it as far as the Carpet Museum when the clouds gave up all pretence and released a full downpour. Shrieking with laughter, they sprinted for a bus shelter, where a freezing wind drove the rain sideways.

Soaked to the skin, Murad concluded that the moment would never be more ridiculous, and therefore might as well be now. He dropped to one knee, fumbled the box open — and watched, in slow motion, as the ring slipped from his numb fingers into a muddy puddle.

Neither of them breathed. Then Aysel crouched, retrieved the ring from the murky water, wiped it on her sleeve and slid it onto her finger.

“For the record,” she said, “I'd marry you come rain or shine. This just proves it.”

An elderly man waiting for the number 88 began to applaud, and beyond the shelter, almost reluctantly, the clouds started to part.

questions.q: What is the central irony of the story?
options: Aysel says no despite the beautiful weather
The perfect forecast is wrong, yet the messy moment works perfectly
Murad forgets the ring at home
questions.why: Nothing goes to plan, but Aysel says the rain “just proves it”.
